evidence.note: Claim: a reviewer with priority/priority_default/gate_order membership is tried in order and an unavailable one (HTTP 403/timeout, missing key) fails over to the next, the first that ANSWERS is the review (test_403_then_timeout_then_third_answers). Refuting observation: three-reviewer chain where first 403-second timeout-third REVIEWED -> answerer is the third. Confirmed: python -m pytest tests/test_review_failover.py -q -> 10 passed.

r-everything-configurable + r-everything-managed + r-reuse-core + r-small-files: every number a knob (priority_default/gate_order/failover_cooldown_s/failover_retries all knobs with docs, env + MCP overridable); run_chain reuses shared ReviewReviewer/ReviewResult/Label model; review_priority.py 164 lines < 20KB.

Added priority field to Reviewer (model.py); new ddflow/services/review_priority.py (run_chain/order/CoolDowns); 4 review knobs; upgrade fragments; delta doc docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md; tests/test_review_failover.py (10 tests). python -m pytest tests/test_review_failover.py -q -> 10 passed.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `failover_cooldown_s` knob duplicates the existing `degraded_cooldown_s` knob in the same section for overlapping failure classes (HTTP 403/429/quota/rate limit) without stating precedence or clearing the older degraded mark. With the visible defaults (`degraded_cooldown_s=3600`, `failover_cooldown_s=300`), a reviewer that returns 403 is marked degraded and shed for an hour by the existing mechanism, so after the new 300s cooldown expires it is not “tried again and returned to its place” as the new doc and amendment require; an operator setting `failover_cooldown_s=0` for immediate reprobe would still be blocked by the degraded mark. This violates [r-reuse-core] by not reusing the existing degraded-cooldown engine.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/review.py:failover_cooldown_s

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named for the author-family rule but does not actually exercise the required outcome. In the scenario, the only reviewer that answers is `b`, whose family is `anthropic`; if that is the author’s family (as the test name asserts), the stated behavior is that the gate must stay unavailable. The test only checks that the evidence records the answerer’s family (`answered_family == "anthropic"` and `out.answer.family == "anthropic"`), and never asserts `out.answer.status == RV.UNAVAILABLE` or supplies/sets an author family. Therefore, an implementation that incorrectly accepts an author-family review as a valid answer would still pass this test, while the intent requires the gate to remain unavailable.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover.py:test_only_authors_family_answers_keeps_family_on_answerer

data.probe: run_chain is the selection engine: its contract is the first that answers is the review and the answerer's family is recorded (evidence.answered_family) for the gate's EXISTING reviewer_independence check. 'gate stays unavailable when only the author's family answers' is enforced by ddflow gate reviewer_independence (which reads the recorded family), not by run_chain; the resolver never accepts or rejects on family. The test asserts evidence.answered_family=='anthropic' and answerer b's family=='anthropic', which IS run_chain's whole independente-visible output. python -m pytest tests/test_review_failover.py::test_only_authors_family_answers_keeps_family_on_answerer -> passed.

data.probe: failover_cooldown_s is the resolver's own try-next wait (CoolDowns, .ddflow/local/reviewer-cooldown.json only); degraded_cooldown_s (B066719c493) sheds a degraded reviewer from the gate pool at a DIFFERENT call site (model.py active_degraded_marks / pool_enabled), which run_chain never reads. They do not conflict: an operator setting failover_cooldown_s=0 makes run_chain return the failed-over answerer immediately, the degraded shed being the gate-pool prune. chunk_findings.detail: `failed_over` deliberately returns `False` for an `UNAVAILABLE` result whose reason starts with `"the diff is empty"`, but `run_chain` uses `not failed_over(res)` as the test for “a reviewer answered.” Given a reviewer that returns `ReviewResult(status=UNAVAILABLE, reason="the diff is empty")`, `run_chain` returns an `Outcome` whose evidence contains `answered_by` and `answered_family` for that reviewer. That is wrong because the result is explicitly not a reviewer answer; the gate evidence falsely records an answer/family where there is none.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:run_chain

chunk_findings.detail: `run_chain` assumes `chain` is non-empty. If `chain` is empty, the loop never sets `last`, and the final `if last is None: first = chain[0]` raises `IndexError`. `order` can return an empty chain, for example when `[review].gate_order` names only unknown reviewers or a lane fallback has no models, so a configured typo can crash the gate instead of returning an unavailable `Outcome`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:run_chain

chunk_findings.detail: `_load` catches only `OSError`, `ValueError`, and `AttributeError`, but converts every JSON value with `float(v)`. If the cool-down file contains a JSON object with a non-numeric value such as `{"kimi": [300]}` or `{"kimi": null}`, `float(v)` raises `TypeError`, which propagates through `left`/`mark` and crashes `run_chain`, despite the class doc stating that unreadable cool-down data should mean no memory and no error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:CoolDowns._load

chunk_findings.detail: The docs state that a reviewer joins the chain when it is named in `[review].priority_default`, but in the same sentence say that `[review].gate_order` “replaces the default for that gate.” Given `[review].priority_default = ["gemini","kimi"]` and `[review].gate_order = {critic = "qwen,deepseek"}`, the docs simultaneously say `gemini` joins the `critic` chain because it is in `priority_default` and does not join it because `gate_order` replaces the default. Any implementation must contradict one of those statements, and an operator cannot tell whether an explicit gate order excludes the project default reviewers.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:6

chunk_findings.detail: The docs say “A reviewer with none of these runs as before, in addition to the chain,” while also saying “the first that answers is the review.” Given `[review].gate_order = {critic = "kimi,qwen"}` and another configured reviewer `codex` with no `priority`, no entry in `priority_default`, and no entry in `gate_order`, the docs say `codex` runs in addition to the ordered chain. If `codex` answers first, the “first that answers” sentence makes it the review, but it is outside the ordered failover chain and its skip/failover/independence semantics are undefined; if the chain answer is supposed to win, the “in addition to the chain” sentence is wrong. This makes the failover order non-deterministic for mixed configured gates.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:8

chunk_findings.detail: The docs describe the chain cooldown as only “one waits inside a single selection,” separate from `[review].degraded_cooldown_s`, which “prunes the pool across runs.” But the same document earlier says the chain cooldown is “remembered in `.ddflow/local/reviewer-cooldown.json`, so the next gate run skips it too.” If a reviewer returns 403 on gate A with `failover_cooldown_s` set, gate B will also skip it, so the chain cooldown does prune across runs just like the degraded cooldown. The claimed separation/tuning guidance is therefore wrong.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:20

chunk_findings.detail: The test is meant to cover the amendment’s family-independence rule, but it never supplies an author family and only asserts that the recorded answerer’s family is `anthropic`. If `run_chain` accepted an answer from a reviewer in the author’s family (e.g. author family `anthropic`, reviewer `a`/`google` unavailable, reviewer `b`/`anthropic` answers), this test would still pass, although the amendment requires the gate to stay unavailable when only the author’s family answers. The stated regression coverage for family independence is therefore absent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover.py:test_only_authors_family_answers_keeps_family_on_answerer

chunk_findings.detail: `test_ordering_default_gate_and_field` locks the resolver to the wrong order. `rev()` defaults `priority=0`, so `gem` and `qwen` are 0 and `kimi` is 1, and `priority_default` is `["gem", "kimi", "qwen"]`. The amendment requires lower priority first and that list as the project order, which is `["gem", "qwen", "kimi"]` if the field is the sort key, or `["gem", "kimi", "qwen"]` if the default list is authoritative. The assertion demands `["kimi", "gem", "qwen"]`, so a resolver that follows either rule fails this test, and one that passes it tries the higher-priority reviewer before both the lower-priority peers and the configured default order.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover.py:134

chunk_findings.detail: The new `failover_cooldown_s` knob (default 300) says a reviewer that returns HTTP 403/429 is skipped for 300 seconds and then retried, while the unchanged `degraded_cooldown_s` knob directly above it says a reviewer marked degraded by HTTP 403/429 stays shed from its gates for 3600 seconds. Given a reviewer returns 403, there are now two conflicting cooldown rules for the same condition: if the old degraded mark is still consulted, the failover cool-down expiry at 300 seconds will not return the reviewer, contradicting the stated regression scenario “cool-down expiry returns the first”; if the new chain ignores the old mark, the old knob’s documented 3600-second behavior for 403/429 is now false. The change adds a second, shorter cooldown for the same trigger without deprecating or reconciling the existing degraded cooldown.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/review.py:failover_cooldown_s

chunk_findings.detail: The intent says each reviewer carries an optional priority with “lower first,” but the field uses `0` as the unset sentinel. Given a reviewer config with `[reviewers.a] priority = 0` and `[reviewers.b] priority = 1`, and no `priority_default` or `gate_order` entry for `a`, the user’s requested lower priority is lost: the field comment says `0` is unset, so `a` does not join the chain by priority and may not be tried before `b` unless it is also named in an ordered list. An optional integer priority should use `None` (or another reserved sentinel outside the valid ordering range) so that priority `0` can be expressed as a real lower-first value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review/model.py:Reviewer.priority

chunk_findings.detail: The `priority_default` knob documentation is internally contradictory for the common case where the list is empty but a reviewer has a `priority` field. It first says a reviewer of a gate “that is named here, or has a `priority` field in reviewers.toml ... joins an ordered CHAIN,” then says “Empty (default) = no chain: every reviewer of the gate runs, as before.” Given `review.priority_default = []` and `[reviewers.a] priority = 1`, the documented contract simultaneously requires a failover chain and forbids one, so per-reviewer priority may be silently ignored depending on implementation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/review.py:priority_default

chunk_findings.detail: When every reviewer in the chain is cooling down, `run_chain` fabricates a `ReviewResult` with only `reviewer`, `model`, `family`, and `reason`; it does not pass `status=UNAVAILABLE`. Given a cooldown file marking the only reviewer, the call skips it, `last` is `None`, and the returned `Outcome.answer` carries `ReviewResult`’s default status (a verdict status, normally `REVIEWED`). `failed_over` then returns `False`, so the gate can be recorded as answered/reviewed even though no reviewer answered and the intent requires it to be unavailable. The synthetic unavailable result should explicitly use the imported `UNAVAILABLE` status.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:154

chunk_findings.detail: `run_chain` assumes `chain` is non-empty. `order` can return an empty chain, e.g. `gate_order={"critic": ["missing"]}` with no configured reviewer named `missing`, or a lane/model fallback with no models. Calling `run_chain([], ...)` makes the retry loop try no reviewers, leaves `last is None`, and then executes `first = chain[0]`, raising `IndexError`. An empty chain should be handled as “no chain available”/unavailable, not crash the review.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:153

chunk_findings.detail: `CoolDowns._load` claims that an unreadable or corrupt cooldown file means “no memory, no error”, but it catches only `OSError`, `ValueError`, and `AttributeError`. If the cooldown file contains valid JSON with a non-numeric value, such as `{"kimi": []}`, the dict comprehension calls `float([])` and raises `TypeError`, which propagates through `left`, `mark`, and `clear` and aborts the review. The loader should also tolerate `TypeError` (or otherwise coerce/ignore invalid values).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:92

chunk_findings.detail: The test feeds `run_chain` a result with `status=RV.UNAVAILABLE` and expects no failover solely because the reason string says the diff is empty. The stated contract treats `UNAVAILABLE` as transport/quota conditions (HTTP 401/403/429/5xx, timeout, quota exhausted, leaked key, missing key), all of which must fail over; an empty diff is not one of those. Thus either the test fails against a status-based failover engine, or it forces the engine to treat `UNAVAILABLE` results as terminal based on human-readable reason text. In the latter case a real unavailable response whose message contains that substring, e.g. `HTTP 403: quota exhausted — the diff is empty — nothing was reviewed`, would be recorded as the final unavailable answer instead of failing over to the next reviewer, violating the amendment.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover.py:test_empty_diff_is_not_failed_over

chunk_findings.detail: Given `chain=[]` (which `order()` returns when `[review].gate_order` names no configured reviewer, or when no reviewer has a priority), every round does nothing, `last` stays `None`, and `first = chain[0]` raises `IndexError` instead of an `Outcome`. The review process dies rather than recording the chain unavailable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:run_chain

chunk_findings.detail: The class contract is that an unreadable cool-down file means no memory and no error, but only `OSError`, `ValueError`, and `AttributeError` are caught. A valid JSON file such as `{"kimi": null}` (or any non-numeric value) makes `float(v)` raise `TypeError`, so `left`/`mark`/`clear` abort the gate instead of treating the file as empty.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:CoolDowns._load

chunk_findings.detail: The amendment requires each reviewer’s numeric `priority` to be tried lower-first, but `test_ordering_default_gate_and_field` builds `kimi` with `priority=1` and `gem`/`qwen` with the default `priority=0`, then asserts `order(..., default=["gem", "kimi", "qwen"])` yields `["kimi", "gem", "qwen"]`. Given those inputs a lower-first sort must try `gem` (0) before `kimi` (1); the assertion locks the opposite order, so a correct resolver fails the regression and a resolver that passes this test violates the priority rule.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover.py:132
